paras: The Arcadia moonshine raid shooting took place on the morning of 28 August 1920, when four Oklahoma County and federal officers raided the home of Charles Chandler, a Black farmer, near Arcadia in Logan County, Oklahoma, in search of a still. Chandler, Deputy Sheriff Homer Adrean and federal prohibition officer Stanley F. Weiss were killed, Deputy Claude Tyler was wounded, and Chandler's son was shot and arrested. Who shot whom was never settled in the coverage, and the son's lynching the next night drew the Black press to the case.

Oklahoma County Attorney O. A. Cargill ordered the raid after a reported disorder over moonshine at Arcadia, sending federal officers Weiss and Reed Miller with deputies Adrean and Tyler to the W. T. Walker farm. The farm lay just across the county line in Logan County, where the Guthrie Daily Leader said the officers were 'overstepping their county line limits'. Walker called Chandler, 54 and the father of twelve, 'a quiet, inoffensive negro' who he did not believe was making liquor.

According to the Guthrie Daily Leader, the officers waited at the still overnight and captured Chandler and his son there without a struggle after 7 a.m. Tyler said that Chandler, under arrest, faced him upstairs with an automatic pistol, wounded him in a struggle and then shot Weiss and Adrean through the door. Mary Chandler said instead that Adrean kept prodding her husband with a gun demanding liquor until he grabbed a Winchester, and that someone she took to be Tyler fired from an upstairs window. When the shooting ended Chandler, Adrean and Weiss were dead, and Miller handcuffed the wounded son to a post.

Posses left Oklahoma City for the scene, and the Topeka State Journal reported that a hundred Black men were organizing nearby. Over the objection of Logan County prosecutor Dinwiddie, Oklahoma County officers took the son, Claude Chandler, to Oklahoma City, and Judge Swank said he would act on the removal. On the night of 29 August a mob took Claude Chandler from the Oklahoma County jail, and his body was found hanging west of the city. No report of an inquest into the deaths at the Chandler house was found in the coverage.

The first Associated Press reports called Chandler 'a negro moonshiner' and said Black men armed with rifles guarded his still, a story that ran in Connecticut, New York and Washington. The Topeka State Journal headlined 'Form Negro Mob' and 'Race War May Start Over Raid on Still'. The Guthrie Daily Leader, published in Logan County, printed the landowner's doubts and the widow's statement, reported an empty still of unknown ownership and no liquor in the house, and said who killed whom 'will likely never be definitely settled'.

Black papers came to the case through the son's lynching. The Tulsa Star argued that 'there could be no living witness' to tie young Chandler to any killing, and the Chicago Whip said he was 'not a moonshiner' and had defended his home from an 'unwarranted invasion'. The Black Dispatch held that any crime had been committed in Logan County and that Cargill 'ought to be tried for man-slaughter' for moving the son.

The Guthrie Daily Leader said there were no eyewitnesses to the killings. Tyler, Miller and Chandler's daughter Alberta said Chandler shot both officers, while Cargill blamed the son and Sheriff G. E. Johnson thought Adrean and the elder Chandler killed each other. Chandler's own death was laid to Tyler in one wire and to Adrean in the United Press version. The wire's armed guards do not appear in the local account.

reader.title: Arcadia moonshine raid shooting
bases: Four Oklahoma County and federal officers raided Charles Chandler's home for a suspected still and the shooting left Chandler and two officers dead and his son wounded and arrested (A4, A6, A20); no crowd took part in the raid itself.

AP and UP wires, the local Guthrie Daily Leader, the Daily Ardmoreite, Tyler's statement and Mary Chandler's statement all agree that the raid on 28 August left Chandler, Adrean and Weiss dead and Tyler wounded, though they disagree on who shot whom (A2, A3, A4, A13, A20).

accounts.label: Wire report (AP, via federal officers at Guthrie and the governor's office)
accounts.gist: Chandler, an 'alleged moonshiner', had armed Black men with rifles guarding the approaches to his still, and the officers were killed in a clash with them.

accounts.label: Wire report (Topeka and UP versions)
accounts.gist: Chandler began firing when the officers surrounded his house; Tyler (Topeka) or Adrean (UP) killed him as he lay wounded.

accounts.label: Deputy Tyler
accounts.gist: Chandler was arrested in the house; upstairs he attacked Tyler with an automatic pistol, wounded him and then shot Weiss and Adrean through the door; Tyler did not know whether the son fired, but later was 'morally certain' the son killed both officers.

accounts.label: Local Guthrie Daily Leader account
accounts.gist: Chandler and his son were captured without a struggle at the still and marched to the house; after that 'all stories' conflicted, there were no eyewitnesses, and the paper doubted the son killed either officer.

accounts.label: Oklahoma County officials
accounts.gist: County Attorney Cargill believed the son killed both officers; Sheriff Johnson thought the son killed Weiss and that Adrean and the elder Chandler killed each other.

accounts.label: Mary Chandler (widow)
accounts.gist: Four officers arrested her husband at breakfast and Adrean kept prodding him with a gun demanding liquor; he grabbed a Winchester, fired twice and ran, about twenty shots followed, someone (she thought Tyler) fired from upstairs, and her son did not fire.

accounts.label: Black correspondent (Tulsa Star)
accounts.gist: The father was arrested and left with two officers, all three were found dead, and the son was seized while trying to leave; with no living witness, nothing connected the son to the killings.

framing.detail: AP wires headlined 'Three Slain in Rum War' and 'Four Killed in Raid on Moonshine Still', calling Chandler a 'negro moonshiner' or 'alleged moonshiner' and repeating that armed negroes guarded the still.
The Topeka State Journal headlined 'Form Negro Mob / Race War May Start Over Raid on Still' and reported that 'one hundred negroes' were organizing.

The Guthrie Daily Leader, in Logan County, noted Oklahoma County officers 'overstepping their county line limits', printed doubts from the landowner and the widow's account, and said who killed whom would 'likely never be definitely settled'.
The Chicago Whip said Chandler's son was defending his home from 'unwarranted invasion' and called the officers' action 'unjustified'; the Tulsa Star said no witness tied the son to the killings.
The Black Dispatch editorial argued that any crime had been committed in Logan County and that County Attorney Cargill 'ought to be tried for man-slaughter' for bringing the son to Oklahoma County.

info: Saturday morning, 28 August 1920, about 7 or 7:30 a.m., after the officers lay in wait overnight

Chandler home on the W. T. Walker farm, about two miles north of Arcadia, Springvale township, just across the Oklahoma County line in Logan County; the Guthrie Daily Leader also placed it south and west of Meridian
Charles (Charlie) Chandler, Black, aged 54, father of twelve, killed; his son (Austin, aged 18, in the first Guthrie report; Claude in later reports) wounded and arrested
Accused of operating a moonshine still; the family and the landowner denied it, and an empty still of unknown ownership was found 100 yards from the house with no liquor in the house
Oklahoma County deputy sheriffs Homer Adrean and Claude Tyler and federal prohibition enforcement officers Stanley F. Weiss and Reed Miller, sent by Oklahoma County Attorney O. A. Cargill
The son, Claude Chandler, held in the Oklahoma County jail on suspicion of killing the officers, was taken from the jail by a mob on the night of 29 August and found hanged (a separate episode)
